questions.subject: PYTHON
questions.learningObjective: trace the order in which a guarded body, its handler, and its cleanup run
questions.stem:
The guarded body prints one line and then raises a fault that a matching handler catches. What does this program print?

try:
    print("start")
    raise ValueError("bad")
except ValueError as err:
    print("caught", type(err).__name__)
finally:
    print("done")

options.text: start, then the caught name, then done
done, then start, then the caught name
options.misconception: believes the cleanup block runs before the guarded body begins

options.text: start, then done, then the caught name
options.misconception: believes the cleanup block preempts the handler when both are present

options.text: the caught name, then start, then done
options.misconception: believes the handler intercepts the first line before the body runs

questions.explanation: The guarded body runs until it raises, printing its first line on the way, and the matching handler then takes over and prints the fault's name, and the cleanup block runs last on the way out no matter which of those two happened. The tempting answers reorder the parts, and the ordering is worth memorising because it is what lets cleanup be trusted: the cleanup block is guaranteed to run after the handler has done its work, never before it.
questions.hint: Follow the three parts in the order the interpreter reaches them: body, handler, cleanup.

questions.stem: A handler clause is attached to one guarded block. Which statement about the faults it intercepts is correct?

options.text: the faults from that guarded body whose type the clause names
every fault raised anywhere in the program, including later code
options.misconception: believes a handler is global once written anywhere in the module

options.text: only the faults that body raises on purpose with a raise

questions.hint: Ask which faults a handler claims and how far its reach extends.

questions.subject: PYTHON
questions.learningObjective: explain the cost of a handler clause that names no type
questions.stem: A function wraps its whole body in a bare handler and returns a fallback value from it. Explain what such a clause hides, and why that makes the resulting program harder to repair than one that stopped.

answer.exemplar: A bare handler claims every fault, not just the one the author had in mind, so a genuine bug such as a misspelled name, a wrong type, or a failed lookup is all reported to the caller as the same tidy fallback. The program then keeps running from a state its author never anticipated, and because the fallback looks like ordinary data, nothing downstream can tell it apart from a real result. A handler that names the type it expects instead lets every other fault propagate to a caller who may be able to do something about it, and it makes the code that survives a fault the code that was actually tested. The bare form is defensible only at a boundary where no further recovery is possible, and even there the fallback should be logged rather than returned silently.

questions.explanation: A bare handler claims every fault, so unrelated bugs are reported to the caller as the fallback value and the program continues from an unanticipated state, which means the failure is both hidden and made harder to find rather than easier. Naming the type confines the claim and lets anything else propagate to a caller with more context. The tempting defence is that a bare handler is shorter, and it is, but the cost is that the reported symptom no longer corresponds to the real cause, so a fault that would have taken minutes to fix now survives as a wrong number.
questions.hint: Ask what a caller can conclude from the fallback value alone.

questions.topic: The Cleanup Block On A Clean Path
questions.learningObjective: trace a cleanup block that runs after an ordinary body completes
questions.stem:
No fault is raised and no handler is attached, but a cleanup block is present. What does this program print?

out = []
try:
    out.append("body")
finally:
    out.append("finally")
print(out)

options.text: the list holding body then finally
the list holding finally only
options.misconception: believes entering a guarded block skips its body when a cleanup block is attached

options.text: the list holding finally then body
options.misconception: believes a cleanup block runs before the body it is attached to

options.text: the list holding body only
options.misconception: believes a cleanup block is skipped when no fault occurs

questions.explanation: A cleanup block runs on every path out of the guarded body, and a body that completes without raising is still a path, so the body appends first and the cleanup appends second. The tempting answer that skips the cleanup when nothing went wrong is the misconception that makes cleanup blocks untrustworthy, and it is worth stating plainly: they run precisely so that the release step cannot be skipped on the boring path, which is the path that happens most often.
questions.hint: A cleanup block is not a handler, so it does not need a fault to be triggered.

questions.subject: PYTHON
questions.learningObjective: explain why a fault raised in a cleanup block displaces the one already in flight
questions.stem: A guarded body raises one fault and its attached cleanup block raises a different one. Explain which fault the caller ends up seeing, and why.

answer.exemplar: The cleanup block is the last thing that runs on the way out of the guarded body, so a fault raised inside it happens while the original fault is still travelling outward. A new fault raised at that point replaces the one in flight rather than joining it, because there is only one slot for the pending fault, and the caller therefore sees the fault from the cleanup block and never learns that the body failed first. That is why a cleanup block should release resources and nothing else: any computation or validation placed there can destroy the diagnosis of whatever actually went wrong. The usual repair is to make the cleanup step incapable of raising, by catching inside it and reporting separately, so the original fault survives to reach a caller who can act on it.

questions.explanation: A new fault raised while another is still propagating displaces the one in flight, so the caller sees the cleanup fault and the original cause is lost, which is exactly backwards from what a cleanup block is for. The block should release resources and do nothing that can fail. The tempting arrangement puts a final check or a report inside the block because it runs on every path, and that is precisely why it destroys the diagnosis: the message a reader finally sees describes the last thing that happened rather than the thing that mattered.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two faults is still travelling outward when the second one is raised.

questions.subject: PYTHON
questions.learningObjective: trace a generator-based context manager through a block that does not fail
questions.stem:
A generator function is decorated into a context manager and the block completes without failing. What does this program print?

import contextlib

@contextlib.contextmanager
def tracked(name):
    print("open", name)
    yield name
    print("close", name)

with tracked("a.txt") as handle:
    print("body", handle)

options.text: open, the body line, then close, in that order
open, then close, then the body line, in that order
options.misconception: believes the release half runs before the body it surrounds

options.text: the body line only, because the decorator discards the prints
options.misconception: believes decorating a generator function stops its body from running

options.text: open and close, with the body line replaced by the handle
options.misconception: believes the block's print is overridden by the name bound to the handle

questions.explanation: The decorator turns the generator into a context manager, which runs the body up to its first yield when the block is entered and resumes after the yield once the block ends, so the open line and the body line and the close line come out in that order. The tempting answer that puts the release first mistakes the generator's shape for a plain function's, and the answer claiming the prints vanished is a useful reminder that a generator's body does not run until something pulls from it.
questions.hint: The first yield marks the boundary between the entry half and the release half.

questions.subject: PYTHON
questions.learningObjective: trace a context manager whose exit reports a true value and hides a fault from the block
questions.stem:
The block raises a fault, and the context manager's exit reports a true value. What does this program print?

class Res:
    def __enter__(self):
        print("enter")
        return self
    def __exit__(self, kind, value, trace):
        print("exit")
        return True

with Res() as handle:
    print("body")
    raise ValueError("boom")
print("after")

options.text: enter, the body line, exit, then after
enter, the body line, exit, then the program stops
options.misconception: believes a fault from the block always escapes regardless of the exit result

options.text: enter, the body line, then the program stops before exit
options.misconception: believes the exit is skipped when the block fails

options.text: enter, the body line, after, then exit
options.misconception: believes the code following the block runs before the release half

questions.explanation: The exit half always runs when the block ends, and it printed its line, and because it reported a true value the fault was marked as handled so the statement after the block ran as well. The tempting answer that stops the program misses what a true result from the exit half means, and it is worth treating that as a deliberate signal rather than a convenience, since it is the one place where a context manager can quietly erase a failure and leave the program running on a state nobody checked.
questions.hint: Ask what the exit half reported, and what a true result there changes.

questions.subject: PYTHON
questions.topic: A With Block On The Failing Path
questions.learningObjective: explain what a context manager does when the block it guards fails
questions.stem: A with block holds a resource and the code inside it fails partway through. Explain what the interpreter does with the block on that path, and what the block's own result then decides.

answer.exemplar: The interpreter leaves the block, and the release half runs on the way out whether the block ended normally, returned early, or failed, so the resource is given back on the failing path just as on the clean one. That is the guarantee the construct exists to provide, and it is why manual cleanup written after the risky statements is unreliable: the failing path is exactly the one most likely to be skipped. The release half then receives the kind of the fault along with the fault itself, and what it returns decides the rest. Reporting a false value marks the fault as handled, so the code after the block runs as though nothing had happened, while reporting nothing lets the fault continue outward to whoever is prepared for it.

questions.explanation: A context manager's release half runs on every path out of the block, including the one where something inside failed, and it is handed the kind of fault so that it can decide what happens next. Returning a true value from it marks the fault as handled and lets execution continue after the block, while returning nothing lets the fault propagate. The tempting assumption is that a with block is only tidier syntax, and the two behaviours above are why it is not, since the suppression case in particular can quietly leave a program running on a state nothing checked.
questions.hint: Ask what the release half is given, and what a true result from it changes.

questions.subject: PYTHON
questions.learningObjective: explain how the else block differs from the cleanup block on a guarded statement
questions.stem: A guarded statement can carry both an else block and a cleanup block. Explain which one covers which outcome, and why choosing the wrong one silently changes what runs when something fails.

answer.exemplar: The else block runs when the guarded body completed without raising, and the cleanup block runs however the body is left, including when it fails. They are not two spellings of the same idea: one reports the successful case, the other guarantees a release step. Putting ordinary work in the cleanup block means it is skipped on the failing path, which is usually the opposite of what was intended, and putting the release step in the else block means it is skipped precisely when the resource is most likely to be abandoned. A third trap compounds both: if the cleanup block raises, the new fault displaces the one already travelling outward, so a release step written there can destroy the diagnosis of whatever actually went wrong.

questions.explanation: The else block belongs to the successful completion of the body and the cleanup block belongs to every way out of it, so the choice between them is a choice about which outcomes the code should run on. Work placed in the cleanup block is skipped when something fails, and a release placed in the else block is skipped when it is most needed. The tempting belief is that the two are interchangeable because both sit beside the body, and the practical cost is a resource that leaks on the failing path or a step that never runs at all.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two blocks still runs when the body raises a fault.
